title: All Work, No Play Is a Problem in Pre-K
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos argues that oral language, not early academic drills, should be the foundation of pre-K and kindergarten. Drawing on her own playful K-1 teaching, Pamela Snow's Language House, Alex Quigley, Anne Fernald and Emily Oster, she suggests that as preschool has become more academic and kindergarten has followed, children who arrive with weak oral language stumble. She cites an Annenberg working paper linking weaker preschool effects to a shift from hands-on, language-rich learning to didactic instruction. She points to Story Champs as a research-backed way to build oral language through storytelling, while insisting she still backs systematic phonics and is not siding with Science of Reading detractors. The question, she says, is when and how to teach, and the practical test is how a classroom makes more time for talking.
points: Oral language is the foundation for phonemic awareness, decoding, vocabulary, comprehension and fluency, so skimping on it weakens everything built on top.
Academic pressure moves down the grades: a more academic pre-K pushes kindergarten to follow, and a child who falters early meets an accelerated pace unprepared.
The Annenberg working paper ties shrinking preschool gains to a move from hands-on language and social learning to didactic teaching of rote reading and math.
Story Champs offers structured, playful storytelling that builds vocabulary, syntax and inference with a substantial research base.
Her case is not anti-phonics: skills can be taught systematically and playfully, and the real question is when and how.
quotes: Oral language is foundational to literacy because long before a child is speaking (and certainly even longer before they are reading), children are listening to their caregivers, and this child-directed speech has been linked to vocabulary growth and processing speed.
Pre-K programs have increasingly adopted some elements of academic instruction, which forces kindergarten teachers to snatch the academic baton and keep the literacy race on pace.

This change from using hands-on learning and focusing on promoting health, language, and social skills to using didactic large group instruction to teach early reading and math skills could account for changes in the medium-term findings across time.
Spencer and Petersen remind us that literacy is language, so systematically building complex oral language skills is academic skill development.

Although I am concerned about overteaching phonics (see The Science of Reading Meets the Science of Learning), I am sold on the importance of systematic phonics instruction. The question is not what—but when and how to teach it.

The point is that for many children, kindergarten is a chance to catch up with peers, so skill-building is indeed important, but that doesn’t mean it can’t be playful, especially if there is an emphasis on oral language development along with developing letter-sound knowledge and phonemic awareness.

Given our time constraints in the classroom, what choices will we make for our youngest learners to give them the best single strategy for setting them up for success? Put simply: How do we make time for more talking?
